description: Creating a project on AI recognition of exo-planets based on their light level.
summary: PlanetX is a web-based tool that uses machine learning to analyze stellar light curves and identify potential exoplanet transit signals. It combines the Box Least Squares (BLS) algorithm with a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) to detect periodic brightness dips and classify signals as confirmed-planet-like or false positives. The project uses real Kepler observations and NASA exoplanet data, with Python, PyTorch, Lightkurve, FastAPI, HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. Its goal is to make exoplanet research more accessible and demonstrate how artificial intelligence can support astronomical data analysis.
details:
Use of Super Intelligence (SI) Tools

During the development of PlanetX, we used ChatGPT as an AI-assisted development tool to support different stages of the project.

ChatGPT was used to:

  • Assist with writing, reviewing, and debugging Python code for astronomical data processing and machine learning.
  • Help understand and implement the Convolutional Neural Network architecture.
  • Support the development and troubleshooting of the FastAPI backend.
  • Assist with frontend development using HTML, CSS, and JavaScript.
  • Help organize technical documentation and clearly explain the scientific concept behind the project.

All AI-generated suggestions and code were reviewed, adapted, and tested as part of the development process. The project concept, implementation decisions, integration, and final evaluation remained the responsibility of the project developer.

AI tools were used as assistants, not as substitutes for scientific research or independent development.

No NASA logos, branding, or official NASA design elements were generated or modified using AI.
PlanetX — Discovering Exoplanets Through Stellar Light Curves

What does the project do and how does it work?

PlanetX is a web-based tool designed to analyze stellar light curves and identify possible exoplanet transit signals. When a planet passes in front of its host star, it causes a small, temporary decrease in the star’s brightness. This phenomenon is known as a transit, and it can be detected by studying changes in a star’s light over time.

PlanetX combines two machine learning approaches to analyze these signals. First, the Box Least Squares (BLS) algorithm searches for periodic brightness decreases that may indicate a planetary transit. If a convincing transit-like signal is found, the light curve is processed and passed to a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN). The neural network then classifies the signal as either a confirmed-planet-like signal or a false positive.

The results are displayed through a simple web interface, making the analysis easier to understand without requiring users to work directly with scientific code.

What benefits does the project have?

PlanetX aims to make exoplanet data analysis more accessible and efficient. Space telescopes collect enormous amounts of stellar data, and examining every light curve manually would be extremely time-consuming.

By combining signal detection algorithms with machine learning, PlanetX helps automate part of this process and makes it easier to identify interesting signals for further investigation. It also provides an educational opportunity for students and astronomy enthusiasts to explore how scientists search for planets beyond our Solar System.

What is the intended impact of the project?

The main goal of PlanetX is to support the exploration of exoplanets by making astronomical data easier to analyze and understand. The project demonstrates how machine learning can be applied to real scientific challenges and how publicly available space telescope data can be transformed into meaningful results.

PlanetX is not intended to replace professional astronomical verification. Instead, it serves as a preliminary analysis tool that can help identify promising signals and encourage further research. In the long term, the project could be expanded to work with larger datasets and observations from different space missions.

What tools, programming languages, hardware, and software were used?

PlanetX was developed using a combination of web development, scientific computing, and machine learning technologies.

  • Python — the main programming language used for data processing, scientific calculations, and machine learning.
  • PyTorch — used to develop and run the Convolutional Neural Network.
  • Lightkurve — used to access and process astronomical light curves from NASA's Kepler mission.
  • Astropy, NumPy, and Pandas — used for astronomical data handling, numerical operations, and dataset preparation.
  • BLS algorithm — used to search for periodic transit-like signals.
  • FastAPI — used to build the backend and connect the machine learning model to the website.
  • HTML, CSS, and JavaScript — used to create the frontend and interactive user interface.
  • NASA Kepler data and the NASA Exoplanet Archive — used as sources of astronomical observations and exoplanet information.
  • Visual Studio Code and Jupyter Notebook / Google Colab — used for development, experimentation, and model training.

The project was developed and tested on a personal computer using CPU-based model inference.

How is the project creative?

The creative aspect of PlanetX lies in combining traditional astronomical signal detection with deep learning in one accessible application. Instead of relying on a single method, the project uses BLS to identify potential transit patterns and a CNN to examine the detected signals more closely.

Another important aspect is the connection between scientific research and practical web development. PlanetX takes complex astronomical data and turns it into a workflow that can be explored through an ordinary website. This makes a topic that is usually associated with advanced research more approachable for people who are interested in astronomy and artificial intelligence.

What factors did the team consider?

During development, several important factors were considered:

  • Scientific reliability: A transit-like signal does not automatically mean that a planet exists. False positives, including signals caused by eclipsing binary stars, must also be considered.
  • Data quality: Real astronomical observations may contain noise, missing values, instrumental effects, and incomplete measurements.
  • Model limitations: The CNN can only distinguish between the two classes it was trained on, and its output should be treated as a model prediction rather than definitive scientific confirmation.
  • Accessibility: The website was designed to make the analysis process understandable and straightforward for users without advanced programming knowledge.
  • Performance: The analysis pipeline was designed to separate signal detection from neural network classification, avoiding unnecessary model predictions when no convincing transit signal is found.
  • Future development: The project was built with the possibility of adding more datasets, improving the model, and supporting additional space telescope missions.

PlanetX brings together astronomy, data science, and artificial intelligence to make the search for worlds beyond our Solar System more accessible.
